posts.quote: A MASON JAR WITH HOLES POKED IN THE LID WAS ALL IT TOOK TO CATCH A WHOLE SUMMER NIGHT.
posts.caption: The first firefly of the evening was the signal, and every kid on the block disappeared into the dusk with a jar. Dad had poked the holes in the lid with an ice pick and warned us not to squeeze. We ran barefoot through the damp grass, cupping our hands around a little blink of light. By the time the porch lights came on, the jar glowed like a lantern on the kitchen table. Mom made us let them go before bed, and we stood on the back step and watched them drift off one at a time.
posts.first: I kept a jar on my windowsill one whole July, and my grandmother never once complained about the grass in my hair. She said a boy who caught fireflies was a boy who paid attention. I think about that every time the evenings turn warm.

posts.quote: Every house on the block had a clothesline, and you could tell the day of the week by what was hanging on it.
posts.first: Monday was sheets, always Monday. My mother pinned them so straight they looked ironed before they ever dried. I can still smell them.

posts.quote: A DIME AND A PHONE BOOTH WERE ALL YOU NEEDED TO CALL HOME, IF YOU REMEMBERED THE NUMBER.
posts.caption: The phone booth stood on the corner by the drugstore with a folding door that never quite closed. You dropped in a dime and listened for the little clunk that meant it had taken. If you were lucky, Mom picked up on the second ring. If not, you stood there with the receiver on your shoulder, counting the minutes you had left. Somewhere in your pocket was a scrap of paper with the number written in pencil, because that was the only place anybody kept it.
posts.first: I had our number memorized by the time I was five, and my mother quizzed me on it at the dinner table. The first time I used a booth by myself I was so proud I forgot to say hello. My dad laughed about that for years.

posts.quote: EVERY CHURCH POTLUCK HAD THREE JELLO SALADS AND ONE CASSEROLE NOBODY WOULD ADMIT TO BRINGING.
posts.caption: The long folding tables came out after the Sunday service, and the whole congregation lined up with paper plates. There was a ham, a pan of scalloped potatoes, and a Jello salad with something suspended in it that nobody could identify. Every dish had a strip of masking tape on the bottom with a woman's name on it. The casserole in the middle of the table always disappeared slowly and from the edges, as if the whole room had agreed to be polite. By the time the pies came out, the preacher was on his second plate and the kids had built a fort under the tables.
posts.first: Aunt Dorothy's green bean casserole showed up every single time, and every single time she said she just threw it together. It was always the first dish scraped clean. I never did get that recipe out of her.

posts.quote: TYPING CLASS / ASDF, JKL; AND A BELL AT THE END OF EVERY LINE
posts.caption: The room was all gray Underwoods in rows, and the clatter was enough to rattle the windows. Miss Henderson walked behind the chairs with a ruler and could spot a peeking eye from across the room. You learned the home keys by feel with a cardboard shield over your hands. Every line ended with a bell and a hard shove of the carriage lever. If you got to forty words a minute with no mistakes, she wrote it on the board, and the whole class pretended not to care.
posts.first: My sister took typing and typed my school papers for a nickel a page. She never made a single error, and I never forgot to pay her. Those old keys had a sound like rain on a tin roof.

posts.quote: YOU HUNG THE SPEAKER ON THE WINDOW, AND THE WHOLE LOT WATCHED THE SAME MOVIE.
posts.caption: Dusk at the drive-in meant finding a good spot on the gravel, not too close to the snack bar. Dad rolled his window down halfway and hooked the heavy metal speaker over the glass. It crackled and hissed until the cartoon started, and then it sounded like the whole world was inside that little box. The back seat was a fort of blankets and pillows, and nobody was supposed to still be awake for the second feature. Somehow we always were.
posts.first: We went every other Friday in the summer, and Mom packed popcorn in a paper grocery sack. I fell asleep before the second feature every time. Dad carried me in and never said a word about it.

posts.character: Values and community (back in five minutes)
posts.quote: A handwritten sign in the shop window meant the owner would be back in five minutes, and everybody believed it.
posts.first: Mr. Albright's hardware store had a card that said 'Back at 2' for years. Nobody worried about it. You just sat on the bench out front until he came walking up the street.

posts.quote: THE MILKMAN LEFT THE BOTTLES AT DAWN, AND NOBODY EVER THOUGHT TO LOCK THE FRONT DOOR.
posts.caption: You could hear the milk truck before you saw it, a quiet hum and the clink of glass in a wire carrier. He came up every porch step in the half dark, set down the cold bottles, and took the empties with the note tucked inside. The cream rose to the top of the neck, and whoever got up first got to shake it. In winter the milk froze and pushed its paper cap up like a little hat. Most mornings he was gone before anybody had their eyes open.
posts.first: Ours was Mr. Kowalski, and he whistled the same tune every morning at the same house. I woke up to it more often than my alarm. When he retired, my mother left a pie on the step with a thank-you note.

posts.quote: SEWING CLASS / A THIMBLE, A PINCUSHION, AND A SKIRT TO FINISH BEFORE JUNE
posts.caption: Every girl in seventh grade got a paper pattern, a yard of cotton, and a seam ripper she came to know very well. The machines stood in a row by the windows, and the room hummed like a hive. Mrs. Dunn checked every hem with a quick turn of her wrist and a look that missed nothing. If your stitches wandered, you pulled them out and did it over until they marched. On the last day of school you wore the finished skirt, and it was somehow the best-fitting thing you owned.
posts.first: My first skirt had a hem that dipped on the left like a ski slope. My mother pressed it and told everyone I had made it myself. I wore it to church in June, crooked hem and all, and felt about ten feet tall.

posts.character: Humor about today vs. then (the road map)
posts.quote: OUR NAVIGATION SYSTEM WAS DAD, A FOLDED MAP, AND A STRONG REFUSAL TO ASK FOR DIRECTIONS.
posts.caption: The map lived in the glove compartment and had been folded wrong so many times that it no longer opened flat. Mom held one corner of it against the dashboard and read street names out loud. Dad drove with great confidence and no particular destination. We passed the same gas station twice, and he said it was a different one. Somewhere around the third hour Mom suggested stopping to ask, and the whole car went silent.
posts.first: Dad once drove forty miles in the wrong direction and told us it was a scenic route. Mom didn't say a word, she just looked out the window and smiled. We got there eventually, and he never admitted a thing.
